title: Adaptive streaming + call choreography: SDK patterns and protocol sketch
body:
Purpose and context:
This is a working sketch for a low-latency, developer-friendly surface that combines streaming token delivery, deterministic tool call choreography, and a schema-first structured output model. The goal is to define pragmatic SDK patterns + a minimal wire protocol we can iterate on in hosted without blocking Dedicated or Private customers.

Why now:
- Customers building interactive assistants keep hitting two pain points: (1) high-latency cold starts when tool calls are detected late in the generation, and (2) brittle client parsing when outputs mix free text, JSON, and tool instructions.
- We can reduce perceived latency and error-surface by making tool intent explicit earlier in the token stream and by standardizing small frame types for event metadata and structured payloads.

High-level design goals:
1) Predictable latency: let clients start rendering UI or call tools before full turn completes.
2) Minimal SDK friction: provide 3 ergonomic levels (raw frames, structured result object, typed helpers for tool invocation).
3) Forward-compatible: wire frames should be extensible; unknown frame types are ignored by older SDKs without breaking tokens.
4) Observability hooks: emit token-level timing and a compact trace for routing and fallback decisions.

Non-goals:
- This doc is not a complete security review. KMS/HSM and enterprise network modes are handled separately.
- Not proposing new model training or new special tokens that need model changes; prefer runtime/SDK-level framing and small prompt conventions.

Sketch: streaming frame types (wire-level)
- TEXT: contiguous tokens that should be rendered as plain output.
- META: short JSON blobs for breadcrumbs (e.g., {event: "tool-intent", confidence: 0.92}).
- CALL_START: announces an intent to call a tool; contains tool_id, schema_reference, and minimal args preview.
- CALL_ARG: one or more frames that deliver serialized args (chunkable).
- CALL_END: finalizes the call envelope and may include a suggested fallback instruction.
- STRUCT: schema-bound JSON payload intended to be machine-readable (complete object; may stream in chunks).
- END: turn finished marker with status.
Notes: frames are small and safe to ignore. The framing layer sits outside free-form text by using an escaping/marker sequence agreed at request-time (a single byte header in streaming protocol or an event type in SSE/WS).

Client ergonomics: 3-tier surface
- Low-level: event stream with explicit frame types. Useful for infrastructure clients, custom UIs. API: onFrame(frameType, payload, meta).
- Mid-level: StructuredResult object with fields: textFragments (list), calls (list of CallIntent objects), structuredData (list of parsed STRUCT objects), trace. This is the default SDK return.
- High-level helpers: "toolRunner" client that can automatically execute CALL_START + CALL_ARG sequences against registered tool adapters and pipe results back as subsequent MODEL_INPUT (optional). This is opt-in.

Example: JS SDK (pseudo)::
const s = redwood.hosted.stream({model: 'x1', prompt});
s.on('frame', f => { if (f.type === 'CALL_START') ui.showToolButton(f.payload.tool_id); });
s.on('structured', r => { // typed helper -> safe JSON
   ui.updateTable(r.structuredData[0]);
});

Example: curl + SSE (pseudo)::
curl -N -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY" -H "Accept: text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"model":"x1","prompt":"list nearby restaurants"}' \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/stream | fgrep 'CALL_START'

Behavioral rules and heuristics:
- Prioritize emitting CALL_START/META early when model shows high likelihood of tool usage.
- If CALL_ARG frames are large, SDKs must provide backpressure APIs (pause/resume) so UI can manage memory.
- When a CALL is emitted, server-side routing should be able to pre-warm tool adapters (where possible) in parallel.
- In case of tool failure, server should emit a CALL_ERROR frame with an error class; SDKs may display a non-blocking error and continue token delivery.

Compatibility and fallbacks:
- Backwards compatibility: if a client does not understand frames, it should still get TEXT tokens in the default stream (frames are interleaved but have explicit deltas so plain token consumers can filter markers).
- For HTTP/1.1 clients, deliver frames as SSE events; for WebSocket clients we use typed messages.
- Provide a "compat" flag that causes the server to emit an aggregated final STRUCT at end-of-turn for older SDKs.

Telemetry and success metrics:
- Primary metric: median time from first token to CALL_START emission when model intent to call tool > 0.7. Target: <150ms additional latency over baseline token generation.
- Secondary metrics: SDK adoption (percent of new hosted integrations using mid/high-level surface), error rate for CALL_* frames, fraction of calls auto-executed by high-level helper.
- UX metrics: reduction in user-perceived time-to-action (A/B test vs current streaming) and fewer parser-related customer bugs.

Security and privacy considerations (notes):
- CALL_ARG frames may contain PII or secrets. Default policy: SDKs and server sanitize logs unless explicitly opted-in (enterprise only).
- Provide a per-request header that toggles whether CALL frames are recorded in trace logs.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Internal alpha: wire + JS low-level SDK, integrate with local tool adapter harness. Collect timing traces (2 weeks).
2) External beta: mid-level StructuredResult default for new SDK endpoints; beta customers opt in via flag (6 weeks).
3) Gradual enable: ‚compat‘ aggregated STRUCT for older clients; add codegen for tool adapters and sample integrations (3 months).

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Complexity vs clarity: more frame types reduce ambiguity but increase surface area for SDKs. Mitigation: provide a single canonical mid-level object that most customers use.
- Model behavior variance: models may not always emit CALL_* markers predictably. Mitigation: combine model heuristics with server-side reranking and small prompt templates.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Should we include a numeric sequence id on frames for reassembly vs relying on stream ordering? (Pros: robust reassembly; Cons: adds header overhead).
- Decide on default sanitization policy and admin controls for logging CALL_ARG.
- Client memory limits: what is the maximum buffered bytes we should accept before dropping or backpressuring?
- Integration with Redwood Console: map CALL_* events to per-route traces and surface them in the timeline.

Appendix: prototype timeline for alpha work items (2-week sprint):
- Week 1: proto wire format, JS low-level SDK, CLI test harness.
- Week 2: mid-level StructuredResult, sample React component demonstrating pre-emptive tool buttons, capture telemetry.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight; please comment on: (a) frame set completeness, (b) SDK ergonomics (do 3 tiers make sense?), (c) telemetry definitions, and (d) rollout cadence.
- Slack thread: #prod-hosted-streaming. I've dropped some quick screenshots and the prototype harness under the linked GitHub PR.

-- Maya
